ideas.expected_net: Arithmetic on deployed capital: discount captured about 1% + trust accrual 2-3.5% a year + merger-announcement pops 1-3% a year - costs 0.3% = 4-7% a year. Only 50-70% of the sleeve is usually deployed because fills are slow, so the sleeve earns about 3-5% a year net, untaxed on market sales. Volatility 2-4%, worst drawdown about -3% to -5%. This cannot approach a levered index: its use is to hold idle cash, or the cash side of a trend filter, at roughly 1.5-3% a year more than a taxed deposit. The pop component rests on my memory of 2021 behaviour, not on anything verified here.
ideas.capital_fit: 10M KRW: works well (0.8M per shell). 50M KRW: works with patience (4M per shell is often several days' volume). 100M KRW: only partly; 8M per shell exceeds normal volume, so expect about half the sleeve deployed. Ceiling roughly 100-200M KRW.
ideas.fake_risks: 1. Fill illusion: displayed size is tiny, so a test that assumes fills at the day's low is fake; use the strict rule above. 2. Floor error: the formula can overstate trust value when a SPAC's trust rate is low or fees are high. 3. The 2021 SPAC mania supplied most of the historical pops and may not recur. 4. Listing-day price rules changed in 2023, so earlier first-day behaviour is not comparable. 5. Holding through a completed merger turns the position into an ordinary small company that often falls below the floor. 6. Halts can lock capital for months. 7. The liquidation payout is taxed as a dividend, unlike a market sale.

top_pick:
Idea 1 (K-NEGLECT) is the pick, as the stock-selection sleeve rather than as a replacement for a levered index core.

- **Why it ranks first:** it is the only one of the three that meets the integrity rules. It uses free date-keyed data from 2010 that includes later-delisted names, has a fixed specification with no fitted parameters, and has a real (if short) pre-2015 period.
- **Where idea 2 fits:** it probably has the stronger edge, but it cannot be tested before 2016, so it is a single blind run. If it passes, it replaces idea 1's ranking step.
- **Where idea 3 fits:** it is where idle cash sits; it is not a growth method.
- **What to expect:** about 8% a year net compound growth from idea 1 alone (range 6-13%). That is roughly level with my forward-looking estimate for the 3x-index-with-trend-filter benchmark (7-9.5% net) and well below the benchmark's realised 2015-2025 history.
- **The more robust conclusion is the mix.** Korean quiet micro-caps and a levered US index are only moderately correlated (I assume about 0.4). On my inputs a 50/50 mix grows about 1 point a year faster than either alone: about 10% against 9.4% and 8.6%.
- **Before any backtest:** confirm that the KRX Open API snapshots include delisted names, that the administrative-issue flag is historical rather than current, and that the key is free of charge.

I ran no backtest and downloaded no price data; every number here is a design estimate.
honest_ceiling:
No method I can design from free data for this investor has an expected long-run net growth of 30-60% a year. My central estimate is 8-11% a year for any single method, 9-12% for a sensible mix, and 15-18% if published edges persist at most of their historical strength. I put the chance of sustaining 30% or more for 10+ years below 3%. Single years of +30% to +60% will occur, perhaps one year in five or six, but that is volatility, not a growth rate.

The arithmetic:

1. Growth limit from Sharpe ratio. With cheap leverage and continuous rebalancing, best-case compound growth = cash rate + Sharpe squared / 2. At a 2.75% cash rate:
 - Sharpe 0.4 gives 10.8%
 - Sharpe 0.5 gives 15.3%
 - Sharpe 0.6 gives 20.8%
 - Sharpe 0.8 gives 34.8%
 - Sharpe 1.0 gives 52.8%
 Because the true Sharpe is never known, half that leverage is the prudent setting: growth = cash + 0.375 x Sharpe squared, which gives 12.1%, 16.3% and 26.8% for Sharpe 0.5, 0.6 and 0.8.

2. What 30% and 60% would need. At half leverage, 30% needs a true net Sharpe of about 0.85 run at about 43% volatility, and 60% needs about 1.24. A free-data retail strategy net of costs is realistically 0.35-0.55.

3. Leverage does not rescue stock selection. Micro-caps can only be levered with margin loans at about 9.1-9.3%. With a 12.5% expected return and 18% volatility, going from 1.0x to 1.5x adds 0.5 x (12.5 - 9.1) = 1.7% of return and costs (1.5 squared - 1) x 0.18 squared / 2 = 2.0% of variance drag, a net loss.

4. Without leverage, 30% growth from stocks at 20% volatility needs about 32% arithmetic return, roughly 24 points a year above the market. That is an information ratio above 2, which only a handful of closed institutional funds have ever sustained.

5. Tax drag.
 - Korean listed shares: 0% on gains, about 0.3% a year on dividends, about 0.2-0.3% a year of sell tax at 100% turnover.
 - US-listed products: 22% of the yearly gain above 2.5M KRW, and to my knowledge losses are not carried forward. For a 34%-volatility strategy with a 17% mean return, expected tax is 22% x E[max(gain - 2.5M, 0)]: about 4-5% of capital a year at 100M KRW, and about 2% at 10M KRW, where the exemption covers the first 25% of return.

6. Benchmark on the same basis. Trend-filtered index Sharpe 0.45 x 34% volatility = 15.3% excess; less 1.9% leverage and fee cost; plus 4% cash = 17.4% arithmetic; less 5.8% variance drag = 11.6% before tax; about 7-8% after tax at 100M KRW and about 9.5% at 10M KRW.

7. What these rates compound to. 12% a year turns 100M KRW into about 310M in 10 years and 3.0bn in 30 years. 30% a year for 30 years would turn it into about 262bn KRW, which is why that rate is not a credible expectation.
assumptions_challenged:
1. "A small investor's best edge is picking stocks." For this investor the larger and more certain edges are in the tax wrapper, not the selection.
 - Korean listed shares carry no capital gains tax.
 - The 2.5M KRW yearly exemption makes the 22% overseas tax almost irrelevant at 10M KRW and expensive at 100M KRW, so the best structure changes with account size.
 - For Korea-listed leveraged ETFs on domestic indices, tax is 15.4% of the smaller of the trading gain and the rise in the fund's taxable base price. One source says that rise is usually small for these funds, so actual tax is often small; check this per fund before assuming the full 15.4%.
 - Korean single-stock futures (282 underlyings from Sept 2026) were outside derivatives capital gains tax according to a 2016 broker note. I could not confirm the 2026 status, so verify with the tax office or KIS before relying on it. Even if still exempt, my arithmetic shows levered Korean large-cap exposure through them grows at only about 8% a year, because the selection edge in large caps is thin and monthly rolls cost roughly 1.5% a year per unit of exposure (my estimate).

2. "US stocks are the natural place for selection." For this investor US single-stock selection is dominated, so I propose no US method.
 - Costs and structure: 0.25% commission a side, currency spread, 22% tax at larger sizes and no margin.
 - Testing: free US price data lacks delisted names. The only clean free test is on Ken French's portfolios, which are built from the full CRSP database, and those are portfolios, not tradeable stock lists.
 - Rough arithmetic for small-cap momentum: 12-14% gross, less 1.2-1.6% trading cost at 150-200% turnover, less about 2% tax at 100M KRW = about 8-10% unlevered. That cannot beat the benchmark.

3. "A long backtest will settle it." It cannot here. Free survivorship-free Korean prices start in 2010 and free fundamentals in 2015. With 8-10% tracking error and about 11 years of holdout, a real 4% a year edge shows a t-statistic of about 1.5-1.8. Honest testing can only reject gross failures; anyone reporting strong significance from this data has searched over parameters.

4. "Tolerance for a -90% drawdown is an advantage." It only helps when a high-Sharpe strategy can be levered cheaply. Stock selection in micro-caps cannot be, so the tolerance buys nothing here.

5. "More signals and a market filter make it better." Each added knob spends scarce statistical power. Idea 1 has three signals, no fitted weights and no timing filter on purpose.

6. Small-capital edges I left out because they cannot be automated or tested under the rules.
 - Equal-allocation IPO subscriptions in Korea (since 2021): worth perhaps a few hundred thousand KRW a year per account, which matters at 10M KRW and is negligible at 100M KRW. Not placeable through the trading API, and no pre-2014 history.
 - Odd-lot priority in US tender offers: Korean brokers generally do not process voluntary tenders for retail holders.
 Both figures are from memory, not checked in this session.

7. Tax facts I checked that differ from common summaries.
 - The large-shareholder line stayed at 5bn KRW per stock (government decision of 15 Sept 2025), although several 2026 guides still say 1bn.
 - The sell tax is 0.20% on both KOSPI and KOSDAQ in 2026.

Sources for this section: https://www.imaeil.com/page/view/2025091517013221198 ; https://studygov.kr/blog/0337-2026-stock-transaction-tax/ ; https://etfshopping.com/guide/etf-tax ; https://www.dailian.co.kr/news/view/1674211 ; https://smallake.kr/?p=12689 ; https://mobile.newsis.com/view/NISX20260511_0003623717

ideas.name: FUT-3VT: trend-gated, volatility-capped S&P 500 exposure through Micro E-mini futures at KIS, cash reserve in USD repo
ideas.mechanism: This is not an alpha. It harvests the same equity premium and trend effect as the 3x-ETF benchmark, through a cheaper tax bucket and with leverage that follows volatility. (1) Tax: overseas futures gains are taxed 11% above 2.5M KRW, against 22% for a US-listed 3x ETF. Korea allows no loss carry-forward, so tax is paid on every winning year; for a 35-45% volatility strategy in a 100M KRW account that is roughly 2-3.5% of capital a year at 11% against 4.5-7% at 22%. (2) Trading cost: one trend switch costs about 1-1.5 bp of notional in MES against 0.15-0.5% in the ETF. (3) Sizing: log growth is L*mu - L^2*sigma^2/2, so 3x does its damage in high-volatility periods; capping exposure at 0.45/sigma removes most of that. Moreira-Muir (2017) support this; Cederburg et al. (2020) find the Sharpe gain is not robust out of sample, so I count only the variance-drag saving. Financing is NOT cheaper: futures embed about SOFR+0.3-0.6% on the full notional, similar to the swap spread inside a 3x ETF, and idle USD margin at KIS earns only 0.7%. Other side: the equity premium is paid by investors who want safety; the futures short side is dealers and arbitrageurs lending balance sheet at SOFR plus a spread. The trend gate works because volatility clusters below the moving average (Gayed-Bilello 2016), a variance effect visible since 1928. The tax and cost edges last as long as the rules do; the premium itself is uncertain.
ideas.instruments: CME Micro E-mini S&P 500 futures (MES, $5 x index; about $38,900 = 52M KRW per contract at S&P 7,770 and 1,341 KRW/USD) in the KIS overseas futures account. Pre-registered alternate run: Micro E-mini Nasdaq-100 (MNQ, $2 x index; about $59,400 = 80M KRW). Cash: USD in the KIS futures account (0.7% deposit rate) for margin plus buffer, the rest in a KIS USD repo (about 3.75% before 15.4% interest tax; a Daishin rate from October 2026, KIS rate to be confirmed). Optional block for 100M+: an unlevered S&P 500 ETF held permanently (Korea-listed in the Kiwoom ISA up to the 20M KRW yearly limit, otherwise US-listed at Kiwoom). One hour of pre-education and three hours of mock trading are mandatory before the first overseas futures order (rule since December 2025).
ideas.rule: Daily, after the US cash close of day t. (1) Trend score g = one third each for P > SMA100, P > SMA200, P > SMA300, where P is the S&P 500 total-return close and SMA includes today. (2) Volatility forecast s = max(sqrt(252*v), 0.8*VIX/100), with v_t = 0.94*v_(t-1) + 0.06*r_t^2 on daily log returns, seeded with the first 60-day variance; before 1990 use the EWMA term only. (3) Target exposure E = g * min(3.0, 0.45/s). (4) Target contracts n* = floor(E * equity_USD / (5 * S&P close)); equity is the futures account plus repo plus any ETF block. (5) Trade only if |n* - n| >= 1 and the exposure gap is at least 0.25x. Exceptions: when g = 0 close everything; if actual exposure (notional/equity) exceeds 3.6x at any US close, sell at the next Globex open down to 3.0x. (6) Execution: marketable order in the last 10 minutes before 16:00 ET of day t+1, one full session after the signal. Backtest fill: day t+1 close, 1 tick (0.25 point) slippage, $1.50 per contract per side. (7) Roll: on the Thursday eight days before the third Friday of March, June, September and December, roll to the next quarter by calendar spread (1 tick). (8) Cash: keep initial margin plus 12% of notional in the futures account (about 55% of equity at 3x), the rest in USD repo, swept weekly. If account equity falls under 1.5x maintenance margin, top up the same day (KIS issues margin calls 08:00-09:00 KST, due 16:00) or halve the contracts. (9) Tax in the backtest: each 31 May deduct 11% of the previous calendar year's positive net derivatives P&L above 2.5M KRW, converted at daily USD/KRW, no loss carry-forward. Variant B (pre-registered, 100M+): hold 50% of equity permanently in an unlevered S&P 500 ETF and set contracts = floor((E - ETF weight) * equity / contract value); futures go net short as a hedge when E is below the ETF weight. Benchmark for every test: daily-reset 3x ETF (3 x index - 2 x (T-bill + 0.75%) - 0.9% fee), held when index > SMA200, else cash, 0.25% per side, 22% tax, same delay.
ideas.data: S&P 500 total return: Yahoo ^SP500TR (1988+), ^GSPC (1927+) with Shiller dividends, or the Ken French daily market return (1926+). Nasdaq-100: ^NDX (1985+). VIX: Cboe or FRED VIXCLS (1990+). T-bill: FRED DTB3. USD/KRW: FRED DEXKOUS (1981+). Futures return is modelled as index total return minus (T-bill + 0.75%) on notional; check against Yahoo ES=F (2000+) and MES=F (2019+). Bias notes: index data has no stock-level survivorship bias. The real bias is country selection (the US is the ex-post winner), so repeat unchanged on Nikkei 225, DAX, FTSE 100 and KOSPI (Yahoo or Stooq); Japan 1990-2012 is the key stress test. Subtract 15% dividend withholding for the ETF benchmark, nothing for futures.
ideas.testable_to_2014: Yes. In-sample 1928-2014 (1990-2014 with the VIX term), blind holdout 2015-2026. MES exists only since May 2019 and E-mini ES since 1997; earlier history is a synthetic future (index minus financing), which is accurate because futures are tied to the index by arbitrage. All parameters above are fixed in advance; nothing is tuned.
ideas.expected_net: Assumptions with a haircut to history: trend score on 70% of the time, volatility while on 12.5-13%, average exposure 2.7-2.8x, S&P excess return while on 8.5% (normal), 11% (central) or 15% (repeat of 2010-2025). Central case: 2.75 x 11% = 30.3%, minus variance drag 0.5 x (2.75 x 0.125)^2 = 5.9%, gives 24.4% while on, 17.3% a year. Subtract 1.5% whipsaw and delay, 1.0% financing spread, 0.3% trading and rolls; add 1.8% on collateral (55% at 0.7%, 45% at 3.75% less interest tax). Pre-tax log growth 16.3%; tax about 11% of an average positive-year gain of 25% = 2.7%; net about 13.5% log = 14-15% a year. Normal-premium case about 9% a year; repeat-of-2010s case about 24%. The same engine gives the 3x ETF benchmark about 7.5%, 12% and 23%. The edge is therefore +1 to +3% a year, mostly tax and trading cost. Variant B adds an estimated 1-1.75% a year. Strategy Sharpe 0.5-0.7, volatility 28-35%, expected worst drawdown over 30 years -55% to -75% (a 1987-type -20% day at 3x is -60% in one session).
ideas.capital_fit: 10M KRW: no. One MES is 52M KRW of exposure, 5.2x of equity, and there is no smaller S&P contract. At this size use the ETF benchmark itself or a Korea-listed 2x ETF in the ISA; the 2.5M KRW deduction makes tax a minor issue. 35-50M KRW: workable but coarse; at 50M, 0/1/2 contracts = 0/1.04/2.08x and the third contract needs about 52M of equity. 100M KRW: yes; 0.52x steps, up to 5 contracts under the 3.0x cap, and Variant B becomes practical.
ideas.fake_risks: (1) Leveraged trend-following on US indices is heavily mined and any test from 2010 measures the bull market, not the rule; the holdout is one regime. (2) The volatility cap gives up return if high-volatility uptrends keep paying, as in 2020 and 2023. (3) Futures are not reset daily: after a -10% day at 3x the account is at 3.9x, and a gap or limit-down lock can exceed the buffer; KIS force-liquidates intraday at its 80% risk ratio. A 3x ETF cannot lose more than the stake; a futures account can. (4) The tax edge depends on the decree rate of 10% (statutory 20%) and on regulators not tightening retail access further. (5) Futures financing richens in stress and at year-end, above the 0.75% assumed. (6) P&L and collateral are in USD, so KRW results carry USD/KRW risk, as the US-listed benchmark does. (7) Pre-2019 results are synthetic, not traded MES prices. (8) Operational: roll errors, API outages at 05:00-06:00 KST, repo-to-margin transfer timing.

ideas.name: Add-on to idea 1: five-market trend overlay with micro futures (gold, crude oil, euro, yen, copper)
ideas.mechanism: Time-series momentum: markets that rose over the last 3-12 months tend to keep rising, and the reverse (Moskowitz-Ooi-Pedersen 2012; Hurst-Ooi-Pedersen 2017 show it over a century). Other side: hedgers, slow-moving allocators and central banks who adjust positions gradually, and mean-reversion traders. The payoff resembles a long straddle: small losses in ranges, large gains in sustained moves, so it tends to pay in slow bear markets when the equity trend gate has idea 1 in cash. Its value here is a correlation near zero with the equity core, which raises portfolio Sharpe; it is not a high return on its own. Why it may not persist: the edge has weakened since 2009 as the trend-following industry grew (industry Sharpe roughly 0.2-0.4 since 2010), and five markets give far less diversification than the 50+ used in the published studies.
ideas.instruments: KIS overseas futures account, CME micro contracts: Micro Gold MGC (10 oz) or 1-Ounce Gold 1OZ (1 oz); Micro WTI Crude MCL (100 barrels); Micro EUR/USD M6E (12,500 euro); Micro JPY/USD (1.25M yen; confirm symbol and listing); Micro Copper MHG (2,500 lb). Listing of each micro at KIS must be confirmed in the product list. Excluded on purpose: equity indices (already in the core), bitcoin (no futures history before 2014), bonds (no micro price contract; the 10-year note future is about $110,000). Gains and losses fall in the same 11% derivatives bucket and net against idea 1 within the calendar year.
ideas.rule: Weekly, after the US close each Friday t, for each market i. (1) Build a daily excess-return series from front-month futures, rolled 5 business days before first notice day (gold, copper, crude) or last trading day (currencies), ratio back-adjusted. (2) Signal s_i = average of sign(cumulative excess return over the last L days) for L = 63, 126 and 252 trading days; values -1, -1/3, +1/3, +1. (3) Volatility sigma_i = sqrt(252) x EWMA standard deviation of daily excess returns with lambda 0.97. (4) Target notional = s_i x (0.07/sigma_i) x equity_USD (7% annual risk per market at full signal). (5) Contracts = target notional / contract value, rounded toward zero; hold 1 contract if the ratio is between 0.5 and 1, none below 0.5. (6) Trade at the US close on Monday (one full session of delay), only if the contract count changes. (7) Guard: if initial margin of core plus overlay exceeds 50% of equity, scale the overlay down pro rata. Backtest costs: 1 tick slippage and $1.50 per contract per side, same tax engine as idea 1. Expected overlay volatility about 12% (7% x average absolute signal 0.75 x sqrt(5)).
ideas.data: Gold: Yahoo GC=F (2000+) or Stooq XAUUSD for longer history, with excess return taken as spot return minus T-bill. Crude: EIA daily NYMEX contracts 1-4 (1983+), which give true roll returns. EUR/USD and JPY/USD: FRED DEXUSEU (1999+) and DEXJPUS (1971+) plus FRED 3-month interbank rates for the carry. Copper: Yahoo HG=F (2000+). Bias notes: Yahoo continuous futures are unadjusted front-month series with roll gaps and occasional bad prints, so roll-adjusted series must be built and spot-checked. The five markets were chosen because micro contracts exist today, a mild selection bias (all five were major markets by 1990). No survivorship issue at instrument level.
ideas.testable_to_2014: Yes, with free data. In-sample 2000-2014 for all five markets (crude and currencies can start in the 1980s-1990s), blind holdout 2015-2026. The micro contracts are recent (MGC 2010, MCL 2021, 1OZ 2025) but share prices with the full-size contracts.
ideas.expected_net: Overlay alone: Sharpe 0.3 (range 0.1-0.45) at 12% volatility = +3.6% a year (range +1.2 to +5.4), minus 0.7% variance drag and 0.6% costs = +2.3% before tax, about +2% after (range -0.5 to +3.5). Alone, with collateral interest, that is roughly 4-6% a year and cannot beat the benchmark. Added to idea 1 at near-zero correlation, portfolio Sharpe rises from about 0.60 to about 0.67 (sqrt(0.60^2 + 0.30^2)); central net growth about 16% a year, with a range of about 9-26% across the three scenarios of idea 1. Drawdowns shrink a little in slow bear markets and not at all in one-day crashes.
ideas.capital_fit: 10M KRW: no. 50M KRW: partly; only 1-3 contracts per market, gold needs the 1-ounce contract, and rounding error is around plus or minus 50% of the intended risk. 100M KRW: yes; roughly 1-7 contracts per market (contract values must be recomputed at current prices), with overlay margin around 10-15% of equity.
ideas.fake_risks: (1) Five markets over 12 holdout years: the standard error of a Sharpe estimate is about 0.29, so a good or bad holdout result proves little. (2) In-sample 2000-2014 contains the gold and commodity supercycle and the 2008 crude collapse, the best trend years on record. (3) Free continuous-futures data quality; copper and gold roll yield are approximated. (4) Liquidity of micro yen and micro copper is thin outside US hours. (5) More contracts, more rolls, more ways for automation to fail; costs double if fills are worse than one tick. (6) The decay since 2009 may be permanent.

ideas.name: VIX futures roll premium, sized for survival: short Mini VIX futures in contango (KIS), with a buy-only VXX put variant (Kiwoom)
ideas.mechanism: Buyers of volatility protection (hedgers, holders of long-volatility ETPs) pay a premium: VIX futures usually trade above spot and roll down. Holders of the front-month index lost roughly 45-50% a year from 2009 to 2025, so a constant short earned about 40% a year on notional at about 65% volatility, Sharpe about 0.6, concentrated when the curve is in contango (Simon-Campasano 2014; Eraker-Wu 2017; Cheng 2019). Other side: insurance buyers who accept a negative expected return for crash protection; that demand is structural. Why it may fade: short-volatility supply has grown (short-vol ETFs, option-selling funds, zero-day options). By my recollection the unfiltered -0.5x product earned only about 11% a year in 2019-2025 with drawdowns near -35% in 2020 and 2025, well below the S&P 500 per unit of risk. The key honest point: the payoff is short convexity and about 0.75 correlated with equities, so it competes with equity leverage for the same crash budget and does not diversify it. Variant B works for a different reason: VXX's real-world decay is a risk premium, not a risk-neutral drift, so it is not priced into VXX options; a put buyer gets the short exposure with a capped loss and pays the implied-volatility premium instead.
ideas.instruments: Variant A: Cboe Mini VIX futures (VXM, $100 x index; about $2,000 = 2.7M KRW per contract at VIX 20; exchange maintenance margin $888 in April 2026) in the KIS overseas futures account. KIS's product disclosure lists the Cboe volatility index among tradable products; whether the Mini is enabled must be confirmed in the product list. Variant B: long puts on VXX (Barclays ETN, not on the PTP list) at Kiwoom, $1.99 per contract, buy-to-open only, taxed as derivatives at 11%; confirm that Kiwoom lists VXX options. Avoid SVXY, SVIX, UVXY and VIXY: they are PTP securities with rolling quarterly exemptions from 10% withholding, unreliable for Korean accounts.
ideas.rule: Variant A (testable). After each US close t read VIX spot S, the front-month VX settlement F1 and the second-month F2 (monthly contracts only). State ON if F1 > S and F2 > F1 on both day t and day t-1; OFF as soon as either fails on one close. When ON hold short Mini VIX futures in F1, or in F2 when F1 has 5 or fewer trading days to final settlement. Contracts = floor(0.125 x equity_USD / (100 x futures price)); resize only at entry, at each roll, or if notional/equity leaves 8-17%. Execute in the settlement window (16:00-16:15 ET) of day t+1. While the sleeve is active the exposure cap of idea 1 is 2.4x, not 3.0x (crash budget: 2.4 x 20% + 12.5% x 200% = 73% of equity). Backtest costs: 0.03 VIX points slippage and $1.50 per Mini contract per side; also report the result for execution at the day t+1 open. Variant B (buy-only). On the first trading day after the third Friday of March, June, September and December, buy VXX puts with the listed expiry closest to 270 days (180-400 allowed) and the listed strike closest to 0.80 x VXX close, spending 2.5% of equity (premium at risk at most 10% of equity a year). Sell 30 days before expiry (Kiwoom force-closes at 02:00 KST on expiry day and does not exercise). No cap reduction on idea 1.
ideas.data: Cboe free VX futures files (2013 to date on the historical data page; the Cboe historical archive is expected to hold earlier contracts back to March 2004, to be confirmed). VIX spot: Cboe or FRED (1990+). VVIX: Cboe (2006+), for the volatility input of Variant B. Rebuild the short-term VIX futures index from futures settlements; do not use ETN prices. Survivorship note: XIV, the product most people backtested, was terminated in February 2018, and the original VXX matured in January 2019 (Yahoo's VXX starts in 2018). VXM launched in August 2020; it is one tenth of VX at the same price.
ideas.testable_to_2014: Variant A: yes. In-sample 2004-2014 (includes 2008), blind holdout 2015-2026 (includes February 2018, March 2020, August 2024, April 2025). Variant B: only partly. There is no free history of VXX option prices, so it can only be model-priced (Black-Scholes on the rebuilt index with implied volatility set to 1.15 x trailing one-year realised volatility, floor 60%, plus a 5% premium haircut per trade). Treat that as indicative, and check live quotes on paper before committing money.
ideas.expected_net: Variant A alone: ON about 78% of days; assumed net premium while ON 32% a year on notional (history about 50%, cut by a third). 12.5% x 0.78 x 32% = +3.1% of equity, minus 0.75% costs (Mini VIX spread is 0.1-0.25% of notional per side, about 30 sides a year) = +2.3%; with collateral interest about 4-6% a year, far below the benchmark. Inside idea 1: sleeve +2.3%, minus 1.9% covariance and variance drag, minus about 2.1% from lowering the equity cap from 3.0x to 2.4x = about 1.7% a year WORSE than idea 1 alone; with the full historical premium it is about break-even. Variant B: assumed return on premium +20% to +60% a year (my rough recollection of 2015-2025 is about +65% on average with total losses in 2018 and 2020) on 10% of equity = +2% to +6%, minus 0.6% variance drag; halved for model risk, +0.7% to +2.7% a year on top of idea 1, worst year -10% of equity. Sleeve Sharpe 0.4-0.7. Worst day for Variant A about -12% to -25% of equity (the front VIX futures index rose 96% on 5 February 2018).
ideas.capital_fit: 10M KRW: no within the risk limit; one Mini VIX is 27% of equity against a 12.5% limit, and one VXX put costs 3-6% of equity against a 2.5% quarterly budget. 50M KRW: yes; 2 Mini contracts, or 1-2 puts per quarter. 100M KRW: yes; 4 Mini contracts. If KIS offers only the full-size VX ($1,000 x index, about $20,000), one contract needs about 215M KRW of equity: not usable.
ideas.fake_risks: (1) In-sample 2004-2014 holds the richest years of the premium (2009-2013). (2) The result is driven by a handful of days; one session's difference in assumed execution changes the answer, so open and close fills must both be reported. (3) The contango filter is the most published rule in this field and is crowded. (4) Mini VIX liquidity is thin outside US hours. (5) Variant B cannot be tested on real option prices with free data; a volatility guess can understate what puts cost. VXX carries issuer and creation-halt risk (March 2022) and reverse splits that leave adjusted, illiquid options. (6) VXM at KIS and VXX options at Kiwoom are unconfirmed. (7) It adds to the same crash exposure as the core; in a 1987-type day both lose together.

top_pick: Idea 1 (FUT-3VT), for accounts from roughly 35-50M KRW upward: the same exposure as the 3x-ETF benchmark, moved into the 11% tax bucket, with 1 bp trading costs and a volatility cap. Its edge is structural (about +1 to +3% a year) and is not a forecast. At 100M KRW add the trend overlay (idea 2) only if it passes the 2015-2026 holdout. I would not run the VIX sleeve (idea 3) unless the holdout shows it beats idea 1 alone; my arithmetic says it is a wash at best. For a 10M KRW account none of the derivative methods fits (one MES is 5.2x of equity); the ETF benchmark, or a Korea-listed 2x ETF in the ISA, is the right tool until equity reaches about 35M KRW.
honest_ceiling:
Realistic expectation: 10-17% a year net; 20-25% only if the next decades are as kind to US equities as 2010-2025. 30-60% is not achievable as an expectation.

Arithmetic. Log growth g = r + SR x v - v^2/2, where v is portfolio volatility; the maximum is r + SR^2/2 at v = SR. Honest net Sharpe for what this investor can run: trend-gated equity beta 0.5-0.65; with a decorrelated overlay 0.6-0.75. Collateral really earns about 2%, not the full T-bill rate. Gap risk (a -20% index day) caps leverage near 3x, so v is about 0.33-0.40, not the Kelly 0.65.
- Central (SR 0.65, v 0.35): 2% + 0.228 - 0.061 = 18.7% pre-tax log. Tax of 11% with no loss carry-forward costs about 3%. Net about 15.6% log = about 17% a year.
- SR 0.5: 2% + 0.175 - 0.061 = 13.4% pre-tax; net about 11-12% a year.
- SR 0.8 (a repeat of 2010-2025): 2% + 0.28 - 0.061 = 23.9% pre-tax; net about 22-23% a year.

What the wish requires. 30% a year net is log 26%, about 30% pre-tax, so SR x v - v^2/2 must reach 0.28: SR 0.81 at 50% volatility, or SR 0.75 at full Kelly (75% volatility), sustained for decades after costs. 60% a year net is log 47%, about 53% pre-tax: SR about 1.0 at about 100% volatility, where one -20% index day at 6-8x leverage ends the account. I know of no public-data, daily, retail-accessible method with a durable net Sharpe above about 0.8.

Probabilities over 20 years for idea 1 (true Sharpe 0.6, volatility 35%, mean net log growth 14%, standard error 0.35/sqrt(20) = 7.8%): at least 30% a year, about 5%; below 0% a year, about 5-10%; a drawdown worse than -60% at some point, more likely than not. The -90% tolerance is consistent with running near full Kelly, but with an estimated rather than known Sharpe, 0.5-0.7 of Kelly is the growth-optimal choice, and the 3x cap already puts the investor about there.
assumptions_challenged:
1. "Futures are cheaper leverage" is only half true. The financing spread in MES (about SOFR+0.3-0.6% on the full notional) is similar to the swap spread inside a 3x ETF, and idle USD margin at KIS earns 0.7% against a T-bill yield near 3.75% inside the ETF. Before tax, all-futures is about 0.5-1% a year WORSE unless the reserve sits in USD repo or part of the exposure is a held ETF. The durable edges are the tax bucket and trading cost.

2. The tax bucket matters as much as the signal. With no loss carry-forward, tax on a 35-45% volatility strategy costs about 2-3.5% a year at 11% and 4.5-7% at 22% in a 100M KRW account. At 10M KRW the 2.5M KRW deduction makes tax nearly irrelevant, so the derivative advantage disappears exactly where the contracts do not fit. Korea-listed leveraged ETFs on domestic indices are widely reported to bear almost no tax on trading gains, because gains on listed shares and their listed derivatives are excluded from the taxable base; I could not confirm this from a primary source in this session.

3. Contract size is the binding constraint, not ideas. MES is about 52M KRW, MNQ about 80M KRW, a Mini KOSPI 200 future (50,000 KRW multiplier) about 35-40M KRW by my estimate of the index level. At 10M KRW no index future fits, and even one Mini VIX is too large for a sane risk limit.

4. The volatility risk premium is not a free add-on. Sized to survive a February-2018 day, a short-VIX sleeve uses the same crash budget as equity beta and earns about the same per unit of it (correlation about 0.75). It is substitution, not diversification. A decorrelated stream with Sharpe 0.3 adds more growth than a correlated one with Sharpe 0.6.

5. Convexity is not an edge. Index option buyers pay the volatility premium. A 12-month SPY call struck 15% below spot costs about 19% of spot (about $14,700 = 20M KRW per contract), gives 4.4x leverage, and embeds a put worth 2.1-2.6% of notional a year. At 3x exposure that is 6-8% of capital a year, against about 1.5% for trend-gate whipsaws. It needs about 35M KRW per contract and has no free price history. Buy-only index calls at Kiwoom are dominated by futures. The only long-option structure I found with a positive expected return is one where the underlying's real-world drift is not in the option price (VXX puts), and that cannot be tested with free data.

6. Backtests of leveraged-long trend rules from 2010 measure the regime, not the rule. Test on 1928 onward (1929-32, 1987, 2000-02, 2008) and on Japan 1990-2012.

7. Also considered and rejected: put-writing on index options (the Cboe PUT index lagged the S&P 500 badly after 2014; leveraged short gamma is the worst tail); overnight-only futures holding (daily round trips cost about 2.5% a year per 1x, which offsets the variance saving); KOSPI 200 option selling (no free data without the exchange login); bitcoin futures trend (no history before 2014).
